title: Valuation convergence of deep p-adic logarithm and exponential series
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime and $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ a finite extension as in [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension], with valuation ring $\mathcal O_E$, maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_E$, normalized valuation $v_E(\mathfrak m_E)=1$ and $e=v_E(\ell)$. Set $v_E(0)=+\infty$ and $|0|_E=0$, and write $v_\ell$ for the normalized valuation of [def-weil-l-adic-numbers]. Use the extended absolute value $|z|_E=\ell^{-v_E(z)/e}$ for $z\ne0$. For every integer $r>e/(\ell-1)$ put $\delta=r-e/(\ell-1)>0$, $q=\ell^{-r/e}$ and $\theta=\ell^{-\delta/e}<1$. For every integer $n\ge1$,
$$v_\ell(n)\le\frac{n-1}{\ell-1},\qquad v_\ell(n!)\le\frac{n-1}{\ell-1}.$$
For every $x\in\mathfrak m_E^r$,
$$v_E(x^n/n)\ge nr-e v_\ell(n)\ge r+(n-1)\delta,\qquad v_E(x^n/n!)\ge nr-e v_\ell(n!)\ge r+(n-1)\delta.$$
Equivalently the two coefficient sequences satisfy
$$|1/n|_E q^n\le q\theta^{n-1},\qquad |1/n!|_E q^n\le q\theta^{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).$$
The series $L(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}x^n/n$ and $A(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n!$ converge uniformly on $\mathfrak m_E^r=\{x:|x|_E\le q\}$. Their sums lie in $\mathfrak m_E^r$, and both maps are continuous there. Thus $\log(1+x)=L(x)$ and $\exp(x)=1+A(x)$ converge uniformly on these domains, with logarithm in $\mathfrak m_E^r$ and exponential in $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$.

source.place: paragraphs 1–2; strengthened coefficient bounds making paragraph 3 evaluable, supplied by Q153

proof.text: Use the extending absolute value and its nonarchimedean inequality from [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-absolute-value]. By [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-integers-dvr], choose a uniformizer $\pi$ and write every nonzero $z\in E$ as $u\pi^k$ with $|u|_E=1$ and $k=v_E(z)$. Since $|\ell|_E=\ell^{-1}<1$, the integer $e=v_E(\ell)$ is positive. For $a\in\mathbf Q_\ell^\times$, the equality $|a|_E=|a|_\ell=\ell^{-v_\ell(a)}$ and the specified normalization give $v_E(a)=e v_\ell(a)$. Also $\mathfrak m_E^r=\pi^r\mathcal O_E$: a product of $r$ multiples of $\pi$ is a multiple of $\pi^r$, and $\pi^r a$ is such a product for $a\in\mathcal O_E$. Thus $z\in\mathfrak m_E^r$ exactly when $z=0$ or $v_E(z)\ge r$, equivalently $|z|_E\le q$.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-2, valuation and ideal normalizations

proof.text: Apply [lem-wf-legendre-digit-sum] with $p=\ell$. If $n\ge1$, its base-$\ell$ expansion has a nonzero digit, so $s_\ell(n)\ge1$, and the identity gives $(\ell-1)v_\ell(n!)\le n-1$. Divide by the positive number $\ell-1$. To bound $v_\ell(n)$, put $k=v_\ell(n)\ge0$, so $\ell^k\mid n$ and $\ell^k\le n$ by the definition in [def-weil-l-adic-numbers]. The inequality $\ell^k\ge1+k(\ell-1)$ follows by induction: it is equality for $k=0$, and multiplying the bound by $\ell=1+(\ell-1)$ increases its right side by at least $\ell-1$. Hence $(\ell-1)v_\ell(n)\le n-1$ as well. Both asserted rational bounds follow, including $n=1$.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-2, the two arithmetic denominator bounds

proof.text:
For $d=n$ or $d=n!$ the previous steps give $v_E(d)=e v_\ell(d)$ and $v_\ell(d)\le(n-1)/(\ell-1)$. Multiplicativity of the absolute value now gives
$$|1/d|_E q^n=\ell^{v_\ell(d)-nr/e}\le\ell^{-r/e-(n-1)(r-e/(\ell-1))/e}=q\theta^{n-1}.$$
This proves the two coefficient inequalities independently of $x$. Since $e>0$, $r>e/(\ell-1)$ implies $r\ge1$, $\delta>0$, $q>0$ and $0<\theta<1$.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-2, uniform weighted coefficient bounds

proof.text:
If $x\ne0$ lies in $\mathfrak m_E^r$, use [lem-sc-dvr-valuation-arithmetic] to compute $v_E(x^n/d)=n v_E(x)-v_E(d)\ge nr-e v_\ell(d)$. Here the quotient formula follows by applying the cited multiplicative identity to $(x^n/d)d=x^n$. The arithmetic bounds imply
$$nr-e v_\ell(d)\ge nr-\frac{e(n-1)}{\ell-1}=r+(n-1)\delta.$$
For $x=0$ both numerators vanish and the same inequalities hold with value $+\infty$. This proves each stated valuation inequality. It also gives $|x^n/d|_E\le q\theta^{n-1}$ for all $x$ in the disc. The logarithmic sign has absolute value $1$.

By [lem-wf-real-geometric-summability] the real family $(\theta^k)_{k\ge0}$ is summable. Multiplication of its finite sums by the constant $q$ commutes with their limit, so $u_k=q\theta^k$ is summable too. All $u_k$ are nonnegative.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-2, a common summable uniform majorant

proof.text:
The field $E$ is complete for the extending absolute value by [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-complete]. Set $S=\mathfrak m_E^r\subseteq E$ and, for $k\ge0$, set
$$f_k(x)=(-1)^{k+2}x^{k+1}/(k+1),\qquad g_k(x)=x^{k+1}/(k+1)!.$$
The estimates already proved show $|f_k(x)|_E,|g_k(x)|_E\le u_k$ for all $x\in S$. Apply the uniform-convergence clause of [lem-wf-dominated-continuous-function-series] to each family, with $K=X=E$ and this $S$. Their partial sums converge uniformly on the entire closed disc to the sums $L$ and $A$, respectively.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-2, convergence of both series with a uniform domain

proof.text: Every term of each series has absolute value at most $q$, because $0<\theta<1$. The nonarchimedean inequality in [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-absolute-value] shows inductively that every finite partial sum has absolute value at most $q$, starting from the zero sum. Passing to the pointwise limits keeps this bound: for a partial sum $s_N$ with limit $s$, $|s|_E\le\max(|s-s_N|_E,q)$, and $|s-s_N|_E\to0$ while $q>0$. Thus $|L(x)|_E,|A(x)|_E\le q$, so both sums belong to $\mathfrak m_E^r$ by step 1.

source.place: Proof paragraph 3, sums remain in the deep ideal

proof.text: Each $f_k$ and $g_k$ is continuous on $S$. Explicitly, for $n\ge1$ and $x,y\in S$, factor $x^n-y^n=(x-y)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x^iy^{n-1-i}$; the nonarchimedean inequality from [lem-weil-l-adic-extension-absolute-value] gives $|x^n-y^n|_E\le |x-y|_E q^{n-1}$. Multiplication by a fixed coefficient therefore preserves continuity; all denominators are nonzero because $E$ contains $\mathbf Q_\ell$. The continuity clause of [lem-wf-dominated-continuous-function-series], with the same summable bound $u_k$, proves that $L$ and $A$ are continuous on $S$.

source.place: Proof paragraph 3, continuity of the sums

proof.text: Define $\log(1+x)=L(x)$ and $\exp(x)=1+A(x)$ on $S$. Adding the constant term $1$ to each exponential partial sum preserves uniform convergence, and translating the logarithm domain by $1$ is an isometry for $d(x,y)=|x-y|_E$. The preceding range bounds give logarithm in $\mathfrak m_E^r$ and exponential in $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$; translation also preserves continuity. These are precisely the last assertions of the item.

source.place: Proof paragraphs 1-3, logarithm and exponential notation and domains
